newsitem.title: USA: Hopes fade for flagging NYMEX Permian gas contract.
newsitem.headline: Hopes fade for flagging NYMEX Permian gas contract.

text.p: Despite high hopes last year for unseating its Kansas City rival, the New York Mercantile Exchange's western gas futures contract has not lived up to expectations and traders saw little chance for a turnaround.
The two contracts have vied for a share of the lucrative West Coast gas market, but after a brief flurry on NYMEX after its May 1996 launch, industry interest has steadily waned.
"It's readily apparent we don't need two contracts in west Texas and the Kansas contract seems to work better," said Chris Eades, gas analyst at UBS Securities in New York.
Eades said the Kansas City Board of Trade (KCBT) contract, launched in August 1995 with delivery at Valero's Permian/Waha hub, grabbed a competitive edge with an early start.
But traders said an increasingly active over-the-counter (OTC) basis market also likely shaved its potential.

"Most of the big companies were used to trading basis differentials against Henry Hub on the OTC, which is liquid enough," said one Houston-based trader, referring to NYMEX's hugely successful first gas contract, which uses Henry Hub in Louisiana as its delivery point.

In addition, he said smaller, independent western producers who could use a Permian contract seemed less inclined than their larger, Gulf Coast counterparts to utilize sophisticated risk management techniques with futures.
While the KCBT contract has not seen explosive growth, there has been steady participation, with open interest varying between 2,000 and 3,000 lots and daily trade this year averaging 330 contracts.

NYMEX Permian has not traded since January 29, when 14 lots changed hands, and has mustered only 8,826 trades since its inception. Currently, there is no NYMEX Permian open interest. In contrast, Hub futures traded almost 700,000 lots last month and have about 160,000 lots outstanding.
"There's a tendency to stay with liquidity and that's Henry Hub," one trader said, noting previous NYMEX failures at launching second gasoline and crude oil contracts.

While early odds favored NYMEX because the same broker could execute cross-regional trades in one pit with reduced spread margins, some traders said the exchange may have miscalculated an industry backlash over its Permian launch.

"NYMEX was arrogant. Kansas City listened to the industry first, and I don't think the boys in Texas liked the idea of NYMEX trying to rain on someone else's parade," said another Houston-based trader.

Some said NYMEX could have better served the industry by offering cross-exchange spread margins with KCBT to boost hedging between the exchanges, then concentrate efforts on launching an Alberta or Rocky Mountain contract.
"If NYMEX wasn't out to squeeze them (KCBT), why didn't they offer (cross-exchange) spread rights?" one said.

NYMEX did launch an Alberta contract last September, but trading there too has flagged. Last week at a gas conference in Calgary, a NYMEX official said the exchange was looking at ways to boost Alberta interest but he offered no specifics.
NYMEX officials were not available for comment this week.
